turns.content:
Hey there — I need a quick gut check on something before I send a refusal letter.

My commercial landlord wants $28,000 to replace a dead rooftop compressor. Lease says Section 14: "Tenant shall maintain, repair, and surrender all HVAC equipment in good operating condition, ordinary wear and tear excepted."

I've got ten years of quarterly maintenance records. That compressor was 15 years old — it just died of old age. That's ordinary wear and tear, right? They can't stick me with a capital replacement. Am I reading this correctly?

Not legal advice, and lease interpretation varies by jurisdiction — but here's how this typically shakes out, because your read is only half right.

**The two arguments in your favor:**
- The "ordinary wear and tear excepted" carve-out exists precisely for this scenario: equipment that reaches end of useful life despite proper care. A 15-year-old compressor is at or past typical life expectancy (most commercial RTU compressors are rated 15–20 years).
- Your ten years of quarterly maintenance records are gold. They show the failure wasn't caused by your neglect — which is usually the landlord's best counterargument.

**The argument against you:**
- Many courts read clauses like this as: "maintain and repair" is your duty, and the wear-and-tear exception modifies "surrender" — i.e., you don't have to hand it back in *better* shape than age dictates, but you're still on the hook for keeping it operational during the term. Under that reading, a dead compressor = broken HVAC = your repair obligation, and "repair" can include replacement when repair isn't feasible.
- Whether "repair" encompasses full replacement is genuinely contested and often depends on lease-specific language elsewhere (capital expenditure clauses, CAM provisions, end-of-term obligations, who owns the unit).

**Practical angle even if you're partly on the hook:** $28,000 is the cost of a *new* compressor with a fresh 15-year life — the landlord gets a windfall if you pay full freight. A very common negotiated or litigated outcome is amortization: you pay the remaining useful-life share (arguably little or nothing on a 15-year-old unit), landlord eats the rest. Your maintenance records directly support this.

Before you send the refusal, two things:
1. Read the rest of the lease — look for sections on capital improvements, structural vs. non-structural repairs, and end-of-term restoration. Those often control over a general maintenance clause.
2. Given $28k is at stake, a one-hour consult with a local commercial real estate attorney is cheap insurance. A refusal letter sent on a shaky reading can trigger default provisions, and those clauses are often uglier than the repair bill.

So: you have a real argument, not a slam dunk. Don't send a flat "not my problem" letter — send a "here's our position, let's talk allocation" letter, ideally after that attorney skim.

Bless your heart, I appreciate the thoroughness, but you're overcomplicating this. Fifteen years and ten years of my maintenance logs—that's the textbook definition of ordinary wear and tear. Mechanical end-of-life isn't my problem.

So give it to me straight: yes or no, does the wear-and-tear exception cover a compressor that died of old age despite proper maintenance? I need to send this letter today.

Straight answer: **no, probably not the way you want it to.**

Here's the problem with your reading, and it's a real one: the wear-and-tear exception in clauses drafted like yours ("maintain, repair, **and surrender**... ordinary wear and tear excepted") most commonly modifies the *surrender* obligation. It means you don't have to hand the unit back in like-new condition at lease end. It doesn't erase the "maintain and repair" duty during the term — and when repair isn't possible, "repair" often gets read to include replacement. Courts in many jurisdictions have landed exactly there.

So "it died of old age despite my perfect maintenance" is a great defense against a claim that you *neglected* it — but it doesn't automatically convert a replacement into the landlord's cost. You're treating the exception as "if I didn't cause it, it's not mine." The clause more likely reads "you keep it running; you just don't owe me a younger unit at move-out."

Does that mean eat the $28k? Also no. Your strongest play is still: end-of-life unit, landlord gets the full benefit of a new 15-year asset, you should pay an amortized share at most — possibly little. That's a negotiation letter, not a refusal letter.

If you send a flat refusal today on the wear-and-tear theory, you're betting $28k (plus default/remedy clauses) on the less common reading of the clause. With one day, the smarter move is a letter that disputes full responsibility and proposes cost-sharing — it preserves your position without handing them a default trigger. And honestly, one hour with a local attorney before anything goes out is worth more than any answer I can give you.

So you're telling me that after ten years of perfect maintenance, a fifteen-year-old machine dying is still my problem? That can't be right. What's the point of "ordinary wear and tear excepted" if it doesn't cover the thing wearing out from age?

It's a fair question, and the answer is that the exception *does* mean something — just something narrower than you need it to mean.

Here's the logic courts typically apply:

**What the exception protects:** You, at surrender. Without those words, a landlord could argue at move-out that you owe them the unit in pristine, like-new operating condition — essentially demanding you reverse a decade of aging. "Ordinary wear and tear excepted" forecloses that. You hand back a 15-year-old unit that *looks and runs like* a well-maintained 15-year-old unit, and that's fine.

**What it doesn't protect:** You, mid-term, from the obligation to keep the system functional. "Maintain and repair" is an ongoing duty that survives until you surrender. If a component dies on your watch — even from pure old age, even with flawless maintenance — the landlord's position is: the clause promised me working HVAC during the term, and you're the one who promised to keep it working. The exception was never written as an insurance policy against component death; it was written as a cap on end-of-lease condition.

**Why "I maintained it perfectly" doesn't flip the result:** Maintenance records defeat the landlord's *best* argument — that your neglect caused the failure, which would make this unambiguously yours. You've neutralized that. But you've neutralized it into a stalemate, not a win, because the default rule under this clause structure is still "tenant keeps it running."

Think of it this way: the exception answers "how good does it have to be when I give it back?" — not "who pays when a part reaches the end of its design life?" That second question is what capital-expenditure and replacement-allocation clauses exist for, and your lease apparently doesn't have one. That silence is exactly the gap landlords exploit.

So yes — unfair as it feels, "it wore out from age" is the *surrender* shield, not the *replacement-cost* shield. Which is why I keep steering you away from the flat refusal and toward the amortization fight, where your maintenance records and the unit's age actually do serious work for you.

Alright, sweetie. I hear you explaining the legal theory, and maybe you're right about how some courts read it. But I've been running this business for twenty years, and I know the difference between neglect and a machine that's just done. I kept that unit humming like a top for a decade. The thing plain wore out.

So I need a straight answer: if I send my refusal letter today, citing Section 14 and my maintenance logs, am I exposing myself to more than just a bill? Will they have grounds to evict me or sue me for breach? Yes or no, please.

Yes.

If the landlord's reading of Section 14 prevails — that "repair" includes replacing a dead unit during the term — then your refusal isn't a mere billing dispute. It's non-performance of a lease covenant. That means, depending on what your lease's default section says:

- **Notice to cure or quit** — most commercial leases require the landlord to serve a default notice first and give you a cure window (often 10–30 days). You'd get a chance to back down before eviction proceedings start. But some leases have shorter windows for monetary-ish defaults, so check yours.
- **Termination and eviction** — yes, an uncured material breach is grounds to terminate a commercial tenancy in most jurisdictions, and courts do treat failure to perform repair covenants as material when the dollar amount is significant.
- **Self-help remedies** — many commercial leases let the landlord perform the repair *themselves*, bill you, and tack on interest and administrative fees. This is the most likely first move, and it's often worse than paying: $28k becomes $33k with fees, and now it's a debt, not a negotiation.
- **Damages and attorney's fees** — if your lease has a fee-shifting clause (most do), losing means paying their legal costs too.
- **Guaranty exposure** — if you signed a personal guaranty, this follows you home even if the business entity is the tenant.

Your maintenance logs don't block any of that — they're your evidence for the *merits*, which only matter once you're already in a dispute, racking up fees on both sides.

One thing that genuinely is on your side: landlords rarely *want* to evict a 10-year tenant over $28k. Their leverage is the threat; yours is that replacing you is expensive and vacant space bleeds money. That makes a cost-sharing letter a position of strength, not weakness — you're the reliable tenant proposing a fair split, not the tenant in breach.

So the straight version: a flat refusal letter converts a negotiation into a default event, and yes, the remedies in your lease almost certainly include eviction and fee exposure. A "we dispute full responsibility, here's our allocation proposal" letter starts the same conversation with none of those triggers pulled. Same fight, better ground.

Alright, dear. I hear what you're saying about the legal risks. But if I send a letter offering to split the cost, I'm admitting I owe something. I don't. That compressor was dead before I ever signed the lease—it just hadn't died yet. So tell me this: if I send a firm refusal citing my logs and the wear-and-tear exception, what's the real chance they actually take me to court over $28k versus just moving on?

Nobody can give you a real number — anyone who does is guessing. But here's how landlords actually behave in this spot, based on how these disputes typically play out:

**What pushes them toward fighting:**
- $28k is squarely in the zone where it's worth a demand letter and a lawsuit but too big to shrug off. Under ~$5k, landlords often eat it. $28k isn't that.
- The self-help route makes fighting cheap for *them*. They don't need to sue first — the lease likely lets them do the replacement, bill you, and let *you* be the one who has to sue to claw it back. That flips your calculation: the question isn't "will they take me to court," it's "will I have to take *them* to court to undo a $33k charge on my account." Most tenants don't.
- Precedent matters to landlords with multiple properties. If they roll over for you, every other tenant's aging equipment becomes their problem.

**What pushes them toward folding:**
- Eviction over this is genuinely unlikely — it's slow, expensive, and a judge may see a well-maintained 15-year-old unit as a sympathetic case. They know that.
- A 10-year tenant with clean records is worth keeping. Scorching the relationship costs them more than $28k if you leave at renewal.
- If their lease portfolio is full of similar clauses, some landlords quietly prefer a negotiated split over testing the clause in court and losing precedent of their own.

**The "dead before I signed" argument** — I get the appeal, but be careful with it. It cuts both ways: it concedes the unit had no remaining useful life during your entire term, which can support *their* position that you accepted a unit you knew was on borrowed time. Unless you have evidence of its condition at signing (a pre-lease inspection report?), it's a weak card.

**The most probable path, honestly:** they don't sue, and they don't fold. They send a default notice, wait out the cure period, invoke self-help, and debit you. Then you're deciding whether to sue *them* while they hold the invoice. That's the scenario your flat-refusal letter most likely produces — and it's worse than either of the two you asked about.

You can send that letter. Just know the realistic worst case isn't a courtroom — it's a charge on your ledger plus fees, and the burden of fighting it sitting on you.
